query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a severe plastic deformation (SPD) treatment followed by a rapid (flash) annealing step to a titanium‐ and nickel‐based high-entropy alloy will refine its grain structure and promote beneficial Ti and Ni segregation at grain boundaries, leading to superior elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to the conventionally processed material.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy with titanium and nickel as primary constituents produced by conventional slow-cooling routes, resulting in a relatively coarse grain structure.
generation.intervention: Perform severe plastic deformation (e.g., high-pressure torsion or equal-channel angular pressing) followed by a short-duration, high-temperature flash annealing treatment to trigger rapid recrystallization and solute segregation at the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Testing under elevated temperatures (approximately 700°C to 1000°C) or extreme-environment regimes relevant to aerospace or nuclear applications; experiments conducted after both treatments and during prolonged high-temperature aging (e.g., up to 100 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: A refined (nanometer-scale) grain structure with stabilized grain boundaries due to preferential segregation of titanium and nickel.
generation.mechanism: The SPD leads to significant grain refinement, and the rapid annealing activates recrystallization while minimizing diffusion-based grain growth. This process enables solute (Ti and Ni) segregation at the grain boundaries, which helps pin these boundaries, reducing grain-boundary sliding and coarsening under high-temperature exposure. This grain-boundary strengthening mechanism is expected to enhance microhardness and yield strength at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy will exhibit higher microhardness and improved high-temperature tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy. Enhancements would be evidenced by a less pronounced drop in hardness after prolonged thermal exposure compared to the baseline processing.
generation.baseline: The alloy processed conventionally, which shows a moderate degradation in hardness (e.g., similar to reported decreases from roughly 1065 HV to 1000 HV after extended high-temperature annealing) due to grain coarsening.
generation.boundary: Restricted to compositions where titanium and nickel are the primary alloying elements in a single-phase state; applicable over the service temperature window of approximately 700°C to 1000°C. It remains uncertain if additional minor alloying elements or impurities could alter the predicted stabilization mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal SPD and annealing parameters to achieve the desired nanostructure without triggering phase segregation remain uncertain. The long-term thermal stability of the ultrafine grain structure under cyclic or prolonged high-temperature conditions is also not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same batch of the titanium- and nickel-based high-entropy alloy. One set is processed by conventional slow cooling (control) while the other set undergoes severe plastic deformation followed by rapid flash annealing (intervention). Subject both sets to prolonged aging at 900°C for 100 hours. Post-treatment, characterize the microstructure (grain size via SEM/TEM) and measure mechanical properties using microhardness and high-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Grain size distribution and average grain size
Microhardness (Vickers hardness) at room and elevated temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SPD plus rapid annealing treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than a ~10% increase in microhardness or yield strength) at elevated temperature compared to the conventionally processed control, or if the refined grain structure degrades rapidly during aging, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
The thermal stability of the grain structure and mechanical properties of the high-entropy two-phase TiCoCrFeMn alloy produced by powder metallurgy, assessed based on microhardness measurements, was analyzed in this work. For this purpose, material obtained via sintering using the U-FAST method was subjected to long-term heating at a temperature of 1000 °C for up to 1000 h in an argon atmosphere. For homogenization times of 1, 10, 20, 50, 100, and 1000 h, grain size changes in the identified phase components of the matrix were assessed, and microhardness measurements were conducted using the Vickers method. It has been shown that the changes in the analyzed parameters are closely correlated with non-monotonic modifications in the chemical composition. It was found that the tested alloy achieved structural stability after 100 h of annealing. A stable grain size was obtained in the BCC solid solution of approximately 2 µm and the two-phase BCC+C14 mixture of roughly 0.4 µm. Long-term heating for up to 1000 h caused the grain structure to grow to 2.7 µm and 0.7 µm, respectively, with a simultaneous decrease in hardness from 1065 HV to 1000 HV.
